source.title: The Grokked Illusion: True Equilibrium Mitigates Catastrophic Forgetting
source.authors: Xiaotian Zhang; Lai-Shun Chan; Yue Shang; Entao Yang; Ge Zhang

page_placements.theme: Delayed robustness and unequal robustness of solved models

record.tranche_reason: Uses modular arithmetic models with saturated test accuracy as a controlled setting for studying robustness to later learning, but does not test grokking's delayed-generalization behavior or the listed versions.
record.gate_note: The models already have 100% test accuracy before the noise-injection fine-tuning. The study measures retention after learning additional noisy data, not when or how test accuracy first rises during grokking. Its grokking-timing and mechanism statements refer to prior work or describe the setup. The noise-retention results are recorded under fits_no_version.
record.test_reason: The study uses already-trained modular-arithmetic transformers at 100% test accuracy as a controlled setting. It measures how much original-task accuracy survives fine-tuning on added noisy data (catastrophic forgetting). It reports no training curves of the initial runs: no delay between train and test saturation, no dependence on dataset size, no circuit formation, no switching via weight norm or initialization, and no optimizer or numerical controls. 'Grokking' is used only as a label for the setting and for the term 'grokked illusion'.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is essentially correct. The authors also name the fragility of conventionally trained, perfectly generalizing models the 'grokked illusion'. In the contributions list they claim the robustness advantage 'arises from' higher effective rank. They later call this evidence correlational.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses modular arithmetic and models with saturated accuracy, but its experiment concerns retention during fine-tuning on added noisy data rather than delayed generalization during grokking.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported retention gap narrows as injected data becomes more structurally similar to the original arithmetic task.

fits_no_version.finding: After memorizing 500 injected noisy samples, WLMD-equilibrium models keep higher original-task test accuracy than AdamW-goldilocks models at the same weight norm (random noise: ~95% vs ~75%). The gap narrows as the noise becomes structurally closer to the task (x+y mod 37: ~100% vs ~97%). Higher effective rank in attention and MLP layers accompanies the more robust models.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Modular-arithmetic models with equal perfect test accuracy differ in robustness to forgetting; higher-entropy (WLMD-sampled) solutions retain more under subsequent fine-tuning.

record.problems: The main comparison uses one pretrained checkpoint per model type, with 10 fine-tuning seeds. The paper reports approximate accuracy values in text without numeric uncertainty for those values. The authors describe the effective-rank association as correlational and say causal links remain to be investigated; the experiments are limited to a controlled modular-arithmetic setting.

untested.parts: Timing of the test-accuracy jump relative to train saturation, and how the delay scales with training-set size. The initial AdamW run (120 epochs, 100% test) reports no curves.
Gradual formation of a generalizing circuit, removal of memorization, and progress measures. The SVD/effective-rank analysis is done only before and after noise injection, not during grokking.
Non-algorithmic data, and switching the delay on or off via initialization scale or weight norm. Weight norm is fixed at 30 and its effect on delay is not reported.
LLM pretraining or fine-tuning; mentioned only as future work.

Weight-decay efficiency account, critical dataset size, and ungrokking. Noise-induced test drops occur in a vocabulary-expanded fine-tuning setup, not by shrinking the training set below a critical size.
The learned algorithm is not identified or compared across runs.
Optimizer or numerical artifacts as causes of the delay are not examined.

record.verdict_notes: Results for AdamW-standard and AdamW-full appear only in an appendix not included in the text. They concern retention, not any grokking version. The Introduction (WLMD ~98%, hardest condition) and the Results and Abstract (~95%, random noise) disagree. Pre-injection quantities come from a single checkpoint per model type; the 10 seeds vary only the fine-tuning.

versions.untested_parts: Does not measure the timing of test accuracy rising after training accuracy saturates, or how grokking delay changes with training-set size.
Does not track formation of a generalizing circuit or memorizing components during grokking, or test whether progress measures anticipate a generalization jump.
Does not test grokking-like delays on non-algorithmic data or whether initialization scale or weight norm switches such delays on or off.
Does not test delayed generalization during LLM pretraining or fine-tuning.
Does not test whether low-norm bias favors an efficient generalizing circuit, or whether a critical dataset size or ungrokking follows.
Does not compare the algorithms learned across runs.
Does not test whether optimizer or numerical artifacts cause grokking delays.

relation.reason: Uses grokking as a controlled setting for a robustness experiment; does not test any listed grokking claim version.

tranche.reason: Uses perfectly generalizing modular-arithmetic checkpoints to compare retention during subsequent noise memorization. Its results measure catastrophic forgetting, with no initial delayed-generalization curves or tests of V1–V7.

source_check.notes: The Introduction reports approximately 98% WLMD retention in the hardest condition, whereas the Abstract, Results and Conclusions report approximately 95%; R2 follows the Results. Ten seeds concern noise injection from single pretrained checkpoints; effective-rank evidence is explicitly correlational.
